title: Snare drum
reference_instrument: Salamander Drumkit snare, 14x6, wires on, overhead microphones (Alexander Holm, CC BY-SA 3.0); the kit copies its sizes, not its materials. The distribution holds one overhead-labelled sample set and does not say whether close-microphone signal is mixed into it, so a line balance measured on it may not be comparable to an overhead-only render
summary: A 14x6 snare from the kit's finite-difference solver, one stroke wires on and one wires off. Shell, hoop and rim don't move, and edge, hoop and shell loss are zero, so wires off the low modes ring too long. Neither clip has the recording's strongest line, and only the wires-off clip has air wall loss. Its two PET heads, air modes to 8 kHz and hickory stick come from sourced cards. The wires are coils of steel music wire pressed into the resonant head, with their count, tension and preload declared. Wires on, the buzz dies like the recording's, though the attack is a little too bright and the tail too tonal. Wires off, the sound is far too dark: 0.0352 % of the first 250 ms lies above 1 kHz, against 1.14 % real.
physics_present: Batter and resonant heads: tensioned PET film with its own bending stiffness and Berger nonlinearity, from a sourced film card
Head film loss: a causal material law on every mode of each head, from a loss curve derived from a published measurement of thin PET film
The exterior radiation load of each head from a baked baffled table, and the viscous boundary layer of the air on both faces of each head
Air inside the drum: cavity modes to 8 kHz coupling both heads
Wall loss of that air, in the wires-off clip only: viscous and thermal boundary layers at the walls, with their square-root-of-frequency law (Pierce 1981, sec. 10-4)
A hickory stick from a sourced wood card, with a Hertz tip transversely isotropic about the grain
Snare wires: coils of steel music wire with the maker's coil dimensions and the wire's measured stiffness and loss, with each coil's thermoelastic, bending and air-drag loss
A viscoelastic Hertz contact between each coil turn and the resonant head's film, in the wires-on clip
An overhead point about 1 m away that hears the drum as one closed body at low frequencies, both heads and a rigid shell over a floor, and crosses over to the baffled path above that
physics_missing: Head edge, hoop, shell and mount loss: stated unknowns, entered as zero
Wall loss of the air in the wires-on clip: 8 kHz still rings at 400 ms, -47.6 dB against -63.7 real

The recording's strongest line in the first 250 ms: 341.3 Hz wires on against 235.5 real, 129.5 Hz wires off against 151.2 real. Wires on, the air's mass lowers the drum to 104.0 Hz late, and its tension hasn't been set again
Spectral balance: the gap is 5.5 dB wires on and 9.7 dB wires off, where two real strokes differ by 0.9 and 1.8. Wires on, 27.4 % of the first 250 ms lies above 1 kHz, against 21.4 % real
Wires-off decay: the gap is 1.51 octaves, where two real strokes differ by 0.67. From peak to -20 dB, 250 Hz takes 550 ms against 200 ms real
A real tail: wires on, 99.3 % of it is in lines against 96.1 % real, led by lines at 164 and 406 Hz where the recording has a cluster at 235 to 505 Hz

The closed body is heard, not felt: the observer is outside the loop, so each head's radiation load is still its own baffled table, with no shell diffraction and no exterior coupling between the heads
Strand-end supports: each strand is pinned at the end plates with no strand-end or cord damping
The wires' count, spacing, length, tension and preload are declared estimates, not sourced
Wire torsion loss is unmeasured and omitted, and the air drag is the linear law, so the wires' loss is a lower bound
Grid convergence: the snare isn't yet converged in grid spacing
The snare is simulated alone, so it doesn't buzz when another drum is struck
On the preset and live routes the strands are plain strings fitted to a recording (96ccf8f1b), not physics
